name: Antares’s top half
intro: This is where the top half of Antares crashed into the Moon on 7 February 1971. It had carried Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell back to their command module, Kitty Hawk, and was then sent back down to make a moonquake. Its crater has not been found.

hotspots.title: Somewhere here
hotspots.text: Antares’s cabin hit between the Apollo 12 and Apollo 14 landing sites. Its crater has never been identified, so this spot is a best guess.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

hotspots.title: Leaving the Moon
hotspots.text: On 6 February 1971 the cabin blasted off from Fra Mauro. Its rocket blast scattered gold foil and shook the flag, as a film camera in the window recorded.

photo.alt: Seen from above through a window, flakes of gold foil fly over the grey ground and a small US flag.
photo.caption: Liftoff from Fra Mauro, filmed from inside Antares as foil flew past the flag.
photo.licenseEvidence: NASA Image and Video Library item S71-19500 (JSC); no third-party credit or copyright notice on the item. NASA: images and video "generally are not subject to copyright in the United States" (https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/).

hotspots.title: The cabin
hotspots.text: This is the front of the cabin, with its pointed windows and docking target. Shepard and Mitchell lived inside it for about 33 hours on the Moon.

photo.alt: Looking up at the front of the lunar module cabin, with a dish antenna and a thin crescent Earth in the black sky.
photo.caption: Looking up at Antares’s cabin from the ladder; the tiny crescent is Earth.
photo.licenseEvidence: NASA Image and Video Library item as14-64-9193 (JSC); no third-party credit or copyright notice on the item. NASA: images and video "generally are not subject to copyright in the United States" (https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/).

hotspots.title: Two listeners
hotspots.text: This crash was recorded by both the Apollo 12 and Apollo 14 seismometers, helping scientists map the Moon’s outer layers.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

funFact: It struck the Moon only about 3.6 degrees above the horizon, almost skimming the ground.
whyLeft: It could not land again or fly home, so after the crew moved out, mission control crashed it to give the seismometers a known shake.
repurpose: Only scattered fragments remain. Finding them would tell engineers how spacecraft break apart in a fast, low-angle crash.
